article_lead.description: a convexity bound that compares a transformed average with the average of transformed values, useful when variation matters

new_bank_questions.title: Two directions of Jensen's inequality
new_bank_questions.body: Let X equal 1 or 4, each with probability one half. Compare E(X^2) with (EX)^2 and E(log X) with log(EX). Explain the opposite directions.
new_bank_questions.answer: EX=2.5, E(X^2)=8.5, and (EX)^2=6.25, so the convex square gives 8.5>=6.25. E(log X)=log(4)/2≈0.69315, while log(EX)=log(2.5)≈0.91629, so concavity of log reverses the inequality. Both are strict because X is nonconstant and each function has strict curvature over the support.

new_bank_questions.title: When Jensen's inequality is equality
new_bank_questions.body: Can Jensen's inequality be equality when X is nonconstant? Give an explicit convex function and explain why.
new_bank_questions.answer: Yes. An affine function such as phi(x)=2x+1 is convex, and E[phi(X)]=2EX+1=phi(EX) for every integrable X. Strict inequality for nonconstant X requires strict convexity on its support.

new_bank_questions.title: A failed Jensen application
new_bank_questions.body: Someone applies E(log X)<=log(EX) to a random variable that equals zero with positive probability. What is wrong with the calculation?
new_bank_questions.answer: The real logarithm is undefined at zero, and a finite E(log X) is unavailable. Jensen's finite-expectation form requires the function to be defined on the support and the transformed expectation to exist.
